qs.q: Aberrant reactivation of which normal developmental microglial function has been implicated in schizophrenia and Alzheimer disease?
qs.e: During development, microglia prune unused synaptic connections via phagocytosis, and aberrant reactivation of this process is implicated in conditions like schizophrenia and Alzheimer disease. Oligodendrocytes and astrocytes handle myelination and metabolic buffering respectively.

qs.q: The positive symptoms of schizophrenia are hypothesized to be caused in part by excessive production and release of which neurotransmitter?
qs.e: The dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia suggests that excessive dopaminergic activity, particularly in the mesolimbic pathway, contributes to positive symptoms. Antipsychotic medications typically work by blocking these dopamine receptors rather than altering acetylcholine.

qs.q: Schizophrenia is thought to be caused in part by excessive production and release of which of the following neurotransmitter agents?
qs.e: The dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia suggests that excessive dopaminergic activity, particularly in the mesolimbic pathway, contributes to the positive symptoms of schizophrenia. Antipsychotic medications work by blocking dopamine receptors. The other neurotransmitters are not primarily implicated in schizophrenia pathophysiology.

rx.name: Schizophrenia
first: An antipsychotic (risperidone, olanzapine or haloperidol) plus psychosocial treatment

ai.subject: Psychiatry
ai.summary: Schizophrenia is a chronic psychotic disorder marked by hallucinations, delusions, disorganized thinking, and negative symptoms. Diagnosis relies on DSM‑5 criteria and exclusion of other causes. Management combines antipsychotics, psychosocial support, and monitoring for complications.

sections.p: Schizophrenia is defined by DSM‑5 as two or more of hallucinations, delusions, disorganized speech, disorganized behavior, or negative symptoms lasting at least six months, with functional decline. Exclude substance, medical, or other psychiatric causes.
b: DSM‑5 criteria: 2+ core symptoms, 6‑month duration, functional impairment

sections.p: Severity is staged by the Clinical Global Impression‑Severity (CGI‑S) and the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS). Staging guides intensity of treatment and monitoring.

Etiology is multifactorial: genetic vulnerability, neurodevelopmental insults, and neurochemical dysregulation. In low‑resource settings, infections (HIV, TB, malaria), malnutrition, and herbal toxins can precipitate or worsen illness.

Patients present with a triad of positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions), negative symptoms (flat affect, alogia, avolition), and cognitive deficits. Early onset (late teens/early 20s) and male predominance are common.
Investigations aim to exclude mimics and assess comorbidity. Prioritize cost‑effective tests and use clinical judgment when unavailable.

t.b: Rule out anemia, infection; abnormal: low Hb suggests chronic disease
Detect metabolic disturbances; abnormal: hyponatremia can mimic psychosis
Identify HIV; positive may alter treatment choice
Screen for TB; abnormal infiltrates require treatment before antipsychotics
Exclude structural lesions; abnormal: mass, encephalitis

sections.p: Red flags include rapid onset, catatonia, self‑harm, or severe agitation. Complications: metabolic syndrome, tardive dyskinesia, suicide, and treatment‑related side effects.
b: Rapid onset (<2 weeks) suggests infection or drug reaction

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first. Antipsychotics are the cornerstone; choose a second‑generation agent for lower extrapyramidal risk. Supportive care includes psychoeducation, social skills training, and monitoring for metabolic side effects.
b: First‑generation antipsychotic (e.g., haloperidol) if rapid control needed; avoid due to EPS risk

t.b: Treat positive symptoms; reduces EPS; monitor weight, glucose, lipids
Reserve for treatment‑resistant cases; monitor neutrophils

sections.p: Regular follow‑up every 4–6 weeks initially, then quarterly. Prevent relapse with medication adherence, psychosocial support, and early detection of prodromal signs.
Schizophrenia is often mistaken for bipolar disorder with psychosis, substance‑induced psychosis, and delirium.
Normal CBC can mask anemia of chronic disease; normal electrolytes may miss intermittent hyponatremia; negative HIV test does not rule out early infection.
b: Anemia of chronic disease may appear normal on CBC

sections.p: Any sudden worsening, self‑harm, or severe agitation requires immediate medical attention.

faq.q: What is the difference between positive and negative symptoms?
faq.a: Positive symptoms add experiences (hallucinations, delusions); negative symptoms remove normal functions (affect, speech, motivation).
There is no cure, but symptoms can be managed with medication and psychosocial interventions.
They have lower extrapyramidal side effects and better metabolic profiles than first‑generation drugs.
